source.title: Prediction in latent factor regression: Adaptive PCR and beyond
source.authors: Xin Bing; F. Bunea; Seth Strimas-Mackey; M. Wegkamp

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports prediction-risk simulations for linear predictors as the number of features p crosses n. This is a different model class and method from the deep-network claim, but the GLS and Ridge results bear on whether prediction risk rises near the interpolation threshold.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are in the p sweep of Figure 1: n=300, K=5, with p in {100, 300, 700, 1500, 3000, 5000}. The text says GLS error diverges when p is close to n and notes GLS and Ridge as exceptions to the general improvement with increasing p near p≈n. Figure values are not stated numerically. Other cited discussions of double descent or interpolation are not this study’s own results. SNR sweeps and other simulations do not test the versions here.
record.test_reason: In a latent-factor linear regression simulation (n=300, K=5), the paper sweeps feature count p across n for the minimum-norm interpolator (GLS). The text says GLS error diverges near p≈n and falls to PCR-K level when p≫n. This is the authors' own result on whether risk improves again past the interpolation point in a non-deep model class (V4).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors say all methods improve as p grows (except GLS and Ridge near p≈n), and that GLS error diverges when p is close to n, citing Hastie et al. They find GLS and Ridge comparable to PCR-K when p≫n, matching their bound that GLS is competitive only when p≫n. They present the benefit of more features as contradicting the classical variance view, attributing it to the factor structure. They do not frame this as a general double-descent claim.
record.recipe_differences: Linear latent-factor regression simulations and new-data prediction risk, rather than deep-network size, epoch, or sample-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported feature-dimension behavior differs near p≈n for GLS and Ridge; the authors also state that GLS and Ridge are comparable to PCR-K when p is much larger than n.

fits_no_version.finding: Under the factor model, all methods (PCR-K, Lasso, ER) improve monotonically as p grows. The authors attribute this to more features carrying more information about A, not to interpolation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In latent-factor data, adding features lowers prediction risk for non-interpolating methods because the signal grows with p (λK(A'A) increases).

record.problems: The relevant risk values are presented only in a figure, with no numerical values or stated uncertainty. The sweep varies feature dimension in a particular factor-regression simulation and does not provide an explicit, quantified fall-rise-fall curve or training-fit measurements.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported simulation results were extracted: the remaining figures vary K, SNR, or use a different simulation setting, rather than reporting the feature-dimension sweep relevant to V4.

untested.parts: First descent / classical U-shape below p=n: the GLS p=100→300 segment shows only a rise. Only one model class (linear min-norm least squares under a factor model) is tested.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
No label-noise manipulation and no multiple peaks. Whether the peak vanishes under optimally tuned ridge is not reported quantitatively (only CV ridge, described as an exception near p≈n).

missing.what: Theoretical risk bounds for GLS give a curve shape on both sides of p=n. Below n (Corollary 7), excess risk scales with (p+log n)/n, rising in p. Above n (Corollary 8 / Table 1), it includes a variance term σ²n/p that falls as p grows. This bears on V4.
Statement that CV ridge selects near-zero regularization when p≫n and so reduces to GLS. This is relevant context for V6 (regularization tuning).

record.verdict_notes: All values are figure-only and the descriptions are qualitative. The 'supports' verdict for V4 rests on the text's statements about divergence at p≈n and later improvement, not on read numbers. The tranche is T3 rather than T2 because this is a new setting (linear factor regression with a min-norm interpolator) giving a result on the claim. Ridge rows are not linked to V4 because ridge is not an interpolating predictor. The ridge 'exception' near p≈n is too vague to label V6.

versions.untested_parts: Training-sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold.
The paper tests a feature-dimension sweep for linear predictors, not a broad set of model classes or a complete, explicitly quantified fall-rise-fall curve across capacity.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample size.
No test of label-noise-driven peaks, multiple descent, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
No re-counting of complexity by an effective number of parameters.

relationships.condition: Minimum-norm interpolating least squares (GLS), latent factor regression simulation, n=300, K=5, p swept 100–5000
relationships.reason: Text says GLS error diverges near p≈n and improves with p beyond, reaching PCR-K level at p≫n (r2, r3–r6). Values are figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: GLS error diverged near p=n, improved as p increased beyond n, and reached PCR-K performance when p≫n.
